body: Big scientific puzzles can start with things you can actually observe. Darwin says studying domesticated plants and animals gave him the “best and safest clue” to how species vary.
evidenceQuote: I have invariably found that our knowledge, imperfect though it be, of variation under domestication, afforded the best and safest clue.

sampleQuestion: Why did Darwin study domesticated plants and animals?
sampleAnswer: He considered those observations a useful starting point for understanding how species vary.

body: A boy got tired of opening and closing a steam-engine valve, so he rigged it to work by itself and went back to playing. Smith says one of that machine’s biggest improvements started with a kid trying to save his own effort.
evidenceQuote: One of the greatest improvements that has been made upon this machine, since it was first invented, was in this manner the discovery of a boy who wanted to save his own labour.

body: A 2,000-year-old call-out for “I’ll do it tomorrow.” Marcus Aurelius reminds himself how many times he has already put things off.

body:
A small fix, a surprisingly big ripple

Smith tells a story about a boy assigned to watch a steam-engine valve. The boy wanted more time to play with his companions, so he tied a string from the valve handle to another part of the machine. That simple connection let the valve open and shut without his constant help.

Smith uses the episode as an example of a machine improvement that began with someone trying to save labour. The passage does not present the boy as setting out to change the world. It shows how noticing a repetitive task and finding a practical way to reduce it can produce an improvement others may value too.
evidenceQuote: One of the greatest improvements that has been made upon this machine, since it was first invented
contextSummary: Smith’s anecdote connects a boy’s effort-saving mechanism to an improvement in the steam engine.
sampleQuestion: What part of the story does Smith emphasize?
sampleAnswer: He emphasizes that one of the machine’s improvements came from a boy who wanted to save his own labour.

body: Sometimes the best productivity hack starts with asking, “Why am I doing this over and over?” Smith’s example is a boy who automated one repetitive motion so he could get back to playing.
evidenceQuote: the valve would open and shut without his assistance
contextSummary: The valve mechanism automated a repeated action that had previously needed the boy’s assistance.
sampleQuestion: What action did the string automate?
sampleAnswer: It let the valve open and shut without the boy’s assistance.

body: Aurelius gives himself a two-part wake-up call:

body: A reminder to act can be more useful than another promise to start tomorrow.

body:
A note to the self that keeps saying “later”

In this passage, Marcus Aurelius does not begin with a grand theory. He begins by confronting his own pattern: he has already delayed these things many times. The reminder is personal, direct, and a little uncomfortable.

Then the passage widens its focus. Aurelius tells himself to understand the world and recognize that he is part of it. Read together, the two moves connect attention to action: notice the habit of postponing, then return to the larger life you belong to. That is the passage’s sequence—not a promise that one reminder fixes everything.
evidenceQuote: how often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the gods, thou hast neglected it.
contextSummary: Aurelius moves from noticing his own repeated delays to reflecting on his place in the world.
sampleQuestion: Is this passage promising that a reminder solves procrastination?
sampleAnswer: No. It records Aurelius confronting his delay and urging himself to understand the world; it does not claim one reminder fixes the habit.
